In Massachusetts v, EPA, the EPA had clearly, and on multiple occasions, 
considered the question of regulating greenhouse gases. It provided a reasoned 
response to the petition for rulemaking which relied upon the extensive study 
by the National Research Council, and its reasons for declining to act invoked 
only legal and broad poUcy grounds, not considerations of agency priorities or 
resources. Providing review in this context seems relatively straightforward. 
Whether that review was “extremely deferential” is, of course, another matter. 
It is worth noting that, in the end, the court’s remedy was cautious. It merely 
remanded for further explanation, specifically noting that it had not reached 
“the question whether on remand EPA must make an endangerment finding, 
or whether policy concerns can inform EPA’s actions in the event that it makes 
such a finding.” And the EPA, for its part, took its time. Although staff drafted 
a proposed rule on motor vehicle emissions that would have responded to the 
Court’s apparent impatience, EPA Administrator Stephen Johnson announced 
that the EPA would not issue a proposed rule, but confine itself to an “Advance 
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking.” Letter from Stephen L. Johnson, EPA 
Administrator, to Hon. Henry A. Waxman & Hon. Tom Davis (Mar. 27, 2008), 
available at https://www.markey.senate.gov/GlobalWarming/tools/assets/files/ 
0451.pdf.
2. The Role of APA Section 555(e). The Supreme Court majority’s 
approach in Massachusetts v. EPA in essence allows a petition for rulemaking 
to turn agency inaction into action. Section 553(e) of the APA allows any person 
to petition for the issuance, amendment or repeal of a rule and section 555(e) 
requires a brief statement of the grounds for denial of any motion or petition 
made in connection with an agency proceeding. From this perspective the court 
is not reviewing agency inaction, but agency action—^namely, the denial of the 
request.
One might wonder whether the APA was meant to be “action-forcing” in 
this fashion. Section 553 on rulemaking, while it contemplates petitions, does 
not itself demand that agencies make any response to those petitions. 
Moreover, the term “agency proceeding^’ used in section 555 is a defined term 
in the APA. According to section 551, “agency proceeding means an agency 
process as defined by paragraphs 5, 7, and 9 of this section.” Paragraphs 5, 7 
and 9 are the definitions of rulemaking, adjudication, and licensing, 
respectively. At the time of a petition for adoption, repeal, or amendment of a 
rule, there is no agency proceeding that is ongoing. The petition is not “in” an 
agency proceeding but instead is a petition “for” an agency proceeding. 
Moreover, even if the APA requires that there be a reasoned response to a 
petition for rulemaking, that alone does not necessarily imply that it is a 
reviewable reason. On the other hand, the Supreme Courts’ reading of section 
555(e) as demanding a reasoned response that is subject to judicial review is 
reinforced by the judicial review provisions of the APA. Section 702 gives a 
right of review to any person aggrieved by “agency action,” which is defined in 
section 551 as “the whole or a part of an agency rule, order, license, sanction, 
relief, or the equivalent or denial thereof, or failure to act.”
